SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL

Priya's SAA-C03 Study Plan (fall 2026)
Plan written: 2026-10-18
Target exam date: Saturday 2026-11-21 (about 5 weeks out), testing center booked, 9:00 AM
Exam format: 65 questions, 130 minutes, passing score 720/1000, multiple choice and multiple response

EXAM DOMAINS AND WEIGHTS
1. Design Secure Architectures - 30%
   IAM users/roles/policies, SCPs, KMS and encryption at rest/in transit, security groups vs NACLs, VPC endpoints, Secrets Manager, WAF/Shield, S3 bucket policies
2. Design Resilient Architectures - 26%
   Multi-AZ, Multi-Region, Auto Scaling, ELB types, SQS/SNS decoupling, Route 53 routing policies, backup and DR strategies (pilot light, warm standby)
3. Design High-Performing Architectures - 24%
   EBS volume types, instance families, caching (CloudFront, ElastiCache), RDS read replicas, Aurora, DynamoDB capacity, Kinesis, data ingestion
4. Design Cost-Optimized Architectures - 20%
   On-Demand vs Reserved vs Savings Plans vs Spot, S3 storage classes and lifecycle rules, data transfer costs, right-sizing, Cost Explorer, Budgets

Time budget: about 8 hours per week on weekdays after work (1 hr x 4 evenings) plus 4 hours on the weekend. Weight my hours toward domain 1 first, since it is the biggest and my weakest.

WEEKLY STUDY GOALS
Week 1 (Oct 19 - Oct 25): IAM deep dive, KMS, S3 security, VPC basics (subnets, route tables, IGW, NAT). Finish the video sections on security. Make flashcards for IAM policy evaluation logic.
Week 2 (Oct 26 - Nov 1): Rest of domain 1 (security groups vs NACLs, endpoints, WAF), then start domain 2: ELB, Auto Scaling, Route 53 routing policies. Hands-on lab: build a 2-tier app across two AZs.
Week 3 (Nov 2 - Nov 8): Finish domain 2 (SQS, SNS, DR strategies, RDS Multi-AZ). Start domain 3: EBS, EFS, FSx, CloudFront, ElastiCache. Take Practice Test 1 on Saturday Nov 7.
Week 4 (Nov 9 - Nov 15): Domain 3 finish (Aurora, DynamoDB, Kinesis) and all of domain 4 (pricing models, S3 classes, lifecycle). Review every wrong answer from Practice Test 1. Take Practice Test 2 on Saturday Nov 14.
Week 5 (Nov 16 - Nov 21): Review weak areas only. Re-read notes, redo flashcards, skim the Well-Architected Framework pillars. No new material after Wednesday Nov 18. Light review Friday, sleep early, exam Saturday Nov 21.

PRACTICE TESTS
- Practice Test 1: Saturday 2026-11-07, 65 questions timed, goal 65% or better
- Practice Test 2: Saturday 2026-11-14, 65 questions timed, goal 75% or better
After each test: log every missed question by domain and write a one-line reason why I missed it.

RESOURCES
- Video course (主 course, sections 1-14) at 1.25x speed
- AWS Free Tier account for labs, set a $10 budget alert first
- Official exam guide PDF and the sample questions
- Flashcards app, 20 new cards per day

PERSONAL RULES
- No studying after 10 PM on weeknights
- If I score below 60% on Practice Test 1, push the exam back one week and rebook
- Keep Sunday afternoons for hands-on labs
notes:
Class notes - Priya (SAA-C03 prep group, session 3)

TOPIC 1: S3 storage classes + lifecycle
- Std = default, 11 9's durability, 99.99% avail, >=3 AZ
- Std-IA = cheaper storage, but retrieval fee + 30 day min, 128KB min billable size
- One Zone-IA = 1 AZ only, 20% cheaper, ok for re-creatable data (NOT for critical backups)
- Intelligent-Tiering = auto moves objs betw tiers, small monitoring fee/obj, good when access pattern unknown
- Glacier Instant (ms retrieval), Glacier Flexible (min-hrs, 90 day min), Deep Archive (12-48 hrs, 180 day min, cheapest)
- Lifecycle rule ex: Std -> Std-IA @30d -> Glacier Flex @90d -> expire @365d
- Versioning + MFA delete for protection; CRR needs versioning on both buckets!!
- exam tip: "unknown/changing access" => Intelligent-Tiering. "rarely accessed, rapid access needed" => Std-IA or Glacier Instant

TOPIC 2: Security Groups vs NACLs
- SG = instance/ENI level, STATEFUL, allow rules ONLY, all rules evaluated
- NACL = subnet level, STATELESS, allow + deny, rules eval'd in number order, first match wins
- stateless => need to allow return traffic + ephemeral ports (1024-65535)
- default NACL allows all in/out; custom NACL denies all until you add rules
- SG can ref another SG as source (nice for app tier -> db tier)
- Want to block a specific bad IP? => NACL (SG cant deny)
- SG changes apply immediately to all instances w/ that SG

TO DO: lab - make a custom NACL, block my own IP, confirm ssh fails, then fix it. Ask instructor about NACL rule number gaps (use 100, 200, 300?). Review VPC endpoints (gateway = S3 + DynamoDB only, interface = PrivateLink for rest).

Quick memory trick: SG = Stateful Guard at the door of the instance; NACL = Neighborhood gate at the subnet border.
photoText:
Whiteboard photo - RDS Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas

Multi-AZ  (High Availabilty / DR)
- Synchronus replication to standby in diffrent AZ
- Standby is NOT readable (except Multi-AZ cluster deploymnt)
- Automatic failover, same DNS endpoint, ~60-120 sec
- Same Region only

Read Replicas  (Scaling reads / perfomance)
- Asynchronous replication => eventual consistancy
- Up to 15 for Aurora, 5 for MySQL/MariaDB [unreadable]
- Can be cross-Region
- Can be promoted to a standalone DB
- Each repIica has its own endpoint

Key Q:  "Need to reduce load on primary from reporting queries" -> Read Replica
"Need automatic failover if AZ goes down" -> Mulli-AZ
Both can be used together!
transcript:
Okay, so, um, let's get started. Welcome back everyone. Today we're going to talk about EC2 Auto Scaling and Elastic Load Balancing, and how those two work together to make an architecture resilient. So, uh, first thing, what problem are we solving? Well, if you have one EC2 instance running your app, that's a single point of failure, right? If it dies, your app is down. And if traffic spikes, that one instance just, you know, falls over. So we want multiple instances, spread across multiple Availability Zones, and something in front of them to distribute traffic. That something is the load balancer.

So let's do the load balancer types. There are, um, basically three you need to know. The Application Load Balancer, the ALB, works at layer 7, so HTTP and HTTPS. It can route based on path, like slash API goes to one target group, slash images goes to another. It can also route on host name and headers. Then the Network Load Balancer, the NLB, works at layer 4, TCP and UDP, super high performance, millions of requests per second, and it gives you a static IP per AZ. And then there's the Gateway Load Balancer, which is for, um, third-party virtual appliances like firewalls. So, this will be on the exam, the difference between ALB and NLB, especially the static IP thing and the path-based routing thing.

Also, side note, I had the worst coffee on the way in this morning, like, the machine at the train station was just broken and I got something that tasted like warm cardboard. Anyway. Moving on.

So, Auto Scaling groups. An Auto Scaling group, an ASG, has a minimum, a maximum, and a desired capacity. You attach a launch template, which says what AMI, what instance type, what security groups, all of that. The ASG then keeps the number of healthy instances at the desired capacity. If an instance fails a health check, the ASG terminates it and launches a new one. And, um, you can use the ELB health checks too, not just the EC2 status checks, which is really useful, because an instance can be running but your app could be totally hung.

Now scaling policies. So, there's target tracking, which is the simplest. You say keep average CPU at fifty percent, and the ASG figures out the rest. There's step scaling, where you define steps based on a CloudWatch alarm. There's scheduled scaling, which is great if you know, like, every Monday morning at nine you get a rush. And there's predictive scaling that uses machine learning on your history. Um, one more thing, the cooldown period. After a scaling action, the ASG waits, by default three hundred seconds, before doing another, so it doesn't thrash up and down.

Okay, a quick announcement before I forget. Lab 4, the one where you build an ASG behind an ALB, is now due Friday, November 6th, by midnight. It was supposed to be earlier, but I pushed it back because a few of you had trouble with the sandbox accounts. So, yeah, Friday November 6th. Please remember to delete your resources when you finish so you don't get charged.

So, to wrap up. Put your instances in at least two AZs, put an ALB in front, attach it to the ASG through a target group, use target tracking for scaling, and turn on ELB health checks. If you do that, you've got a pretty resilient web tier. Um, any questions? No? Okay, good. Let's take a ten minute break and then we'll look at a demo.
lectureTitle: EC2 Auto Scaling and Elastic Load Balancing for Resilient Architectures
